Senses.PreferredTarget: not blind to cause and effect
AlternateTargets: not ignorant of cause and effect
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'not blind to cause and effect' or 'not obscuring cause and effect.' The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong's commentary explicitly contrasts the two phrases: 'not falling into cause and effect is rejecting it through the view of annihilation; not being blind to cause and effect is obtaining the marvelous while following the flow' (不落因果是撥無斷見。不昧因果。是隨流得妙). The same commentary records an objection: 'as for not being blind to cause and effect, he still has not shed the fox body' (只如不昧因果。也未脫得野狐身). Dahui repeatedly answers questions about why the former Baizhang fell into a fox body after saying 'not falling' and why the latter Baizhang's 'not being blind' led to shedding it only by saying, 'just raise it this way to people' (逢人但恁麼舉). Later records continue asking whether 'not falling' and 'not being blind' are the same or different.
Senses.Note: The primary sense is the shared phrase in the historical Baizhang public case, not a Baizhang-specific meaning. The fox-body sequence is translated because the record literally states it; no broader account is inferred from it. Wansong's contrast is reported as Wansong's explicit wording, while the two monks' objection and later same-or-different questions show that the record does not reduce the pair to one uncontested gloss.

AlternateTargets: not lodged in the written word
Senses.Explanation: (不立) = not setting up / not establishing; (文字) = written graphs, letters. It travels as one member of the four-phrase formula of the school — "a separate transmission outside the teachings; not setting up words; pointing directly at the human mind; seeing nature, becoming Buddha" (教外別傳，不立文字，直指人心，見性成佛) — and is bound in the record to Bodhidharma's coming from the West: (達磨西來不立文字) verbatim 16 times in 14 allowlist files, and (不立文字) within ten characters of (直指人心) in 140 places across 87 files. The corpus states what the phrase covers in its own words. (懶菴), quoted in (禪林寶訓): "that the great master Bodhidharma sailed here and did not set up letters made plain the purport of the markless; it is not that Bodhidharma produced a new idea of his own and set up a separate gate" (達磨大師航海而來不立文字者。蓋明無相之旨。非達磨自出新意別立門戶). On the two graphs themselves, the Platform Sutra records Huineng: "those who cling to emptiness slander the scriptures, saying flatly 'use no letters'; but having said 'use no letters,' one ought not speak either — this very speech is the mark of letters" (執空之人有謗經，直言不用文字。既云不用文字，人亦不合語言。只此語言，便是文字之相), then (又云)：『(直道不立文字)。』"even the two graphs (不立) are themselves letters" (即此不立兩字，亦是文字; parallel wording in the Dunhuang-lineage 壇經, T/T48/T48n2007.xml); and (覺浪道盛) asks "is being unversed in letters to be taken as not setting up letters?" (將以不通文字，為不立文字乎哉). Attested deployment: recited as the four-phrase set; spoken under the Bodhidharma ascription in (上堂)/(小參) discourse; and posed as a question — a novice asks (如何是不立文字的佛法) ('what is the Buddha's teaching of not setting up letters?'), and Fazhou Daoji (法舟道濟) calls the novice, who responds, then says "what letters are involved?" (涉甚麼文字 — 天寧法舟濟禪師剩語, J/J40/J40nB491.xml). Attested expansions: (不立文字語句) ('not setting up words or phrases'; 30 hits / 14 files), (不立文字語言) ('not setting up words or speech'; 12 hits / 11 files).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The phrase is pan-Chan; individual masters invoke it rather than own it, so occurrences are attributed to the master using it in his own discourse. Very well attested: 435 raw hits across 188 allowlist files (tag-stripped grep, 2026-07-11). Collocation counts: (不立文字) followed within ten characters by (教外別傳) in 53 places / 47 files, the reverse order in 39 / 32.

Senses.PreferredTarget: not be a companion to the myriad things
AlternateTargets: the one who is not a companion to the myriad things
Senses.Explanation: Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers, including 'Guanyin,' 'Where have all the many people in Hongzhou gone?' and 'passing through a hundred flowers without one leaf sticking to the body.' Yuanwu's instruction explicitly says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' A preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever he raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 446 matches in 153 files. The person-question form has 139 matches in 73 files, while the longer nominal form ending in 'the one who' has 269 matches in 117. Three passages in three files directly ask, 'What is not being a companion to the myriad things?' One text explicitly calls it the public case of not being companion to the myriad things, and one instruction uses the naming formula 'the ancients called him the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' The distribution supports one corpus-wide fixed expression rather than a meaning restricted to Layman Pang, Shitou, or Mazu.

Senses.PreferredTarget: does not fall into cause and effect
AlternateTargets: not falling into cause and effect
does not enter cause and effect
Senses.Explanation: The phrase literally says “does not fall into cause and effect.” Its central corpus setting is Baizhang's real wild-fox public case. An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes a monk's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The entry preserves the case's people, answers, stated five-hundred-life consequence, correction, and later comments without replacing those recorded details with an added theory of cause and effect. The paired abbreviated form “not falling, not obscuring” (不落不昧) occurs 86 times in 45 files; “not falling versus not obscuring” (不落與不昧) occurs 12 times in eight files. No “not dropping into cause and effect” (不墮因果) variant was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 於過去迦葉佛時。曾住此山。因學人問。大修行底人還落因果。也無。某甲對云。不落因果。五百生墮野狐身。今請和尚。代一轉語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's case text records the old man's confession: in Kāśyapa Buddha's time he lived on the mountain; when a student asked whether a person of great conduct still falls into cause and effect, he answered “does not fall into cause and effect,” and for five hundred lives fell into a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang for a substitute turning phrase. As a raised public case with multiple speakers, MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to face or match the occasion. In Chan records it names responsive encounter rather than a private state. One early lamp compilation makes “encounters responding to the occasion” a section heading for recorded cases. A later questioner says that during “questioning and discrimination in responding to the occasion” his responses are not free-flowing, and asks where the fault lies; the master's answer examines him rather than treating interview performance as optional. A recorded dialogue asks where the three vehicles and twelve divisions of teaching were obtained, and the master answers, “they were obtained in responding to the occasion.” Hongzhi speaks of “an eye for responding to the occasion in engaging the world,” followed by the claim that the many conditions cannot bury it. The same verb extends to audience-responsive speech: Gu Xue records that those of sharp capacity are told to investigate Chan and those of middling or lower capacity to invoke buddha, calling this “speaking in response to the occasion,” then asks what is right or wrong. The corpus also uses the term in titles such as collections of hundreds of encounters, in appraisals of a speaker's response, and in compounds with answering and reception. Thus the ordinary graph “occasion” or “capacity” (機) is bent toward the live occasion or capacity presented by another: “respond to the occasion” (對機) means meeting it in an answer, action, exchange, or address preserved by the record.
Senses.Note: “Occasion” keeps the range of the graph “occasion/capacity” (機) without importing a mystical faculty. The heading, question-and-discrimination phrase, direct answer, and “eye” collocation all require an interpersonal responsive sense. Compare “meet the occasion” (當機), “occasion of encounter” (機緣), “question-and-answer” (問答), and “responsive engagement” (應酬); none is simply synonymous.

Senses.Explanation: The paired graphs mean to wander or roam at ease. In a lamp narrative, Tianhuang tells Longtan, “roam at ease according to your nature and range freely following conditions; exhaust the ordinary mind, with no other superior understanding” (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). An Ancestral Hall narrative describes someone “delighting in clouds and waters, roaming at ease whether going or staying” (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Productive forms include “roam at ease and be unbound” (逍遙自在), “range freely and roam at ease” (放曠逍遙), and “roam at ease according to one's nature” (任性逍遙).
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 974 hits in 245 texts. Yongjue gives a direct corrective definition: “what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely” is being aloof and unattached amid every false scene, “like a bird flying through the sky with not the slightest thing tying it, like a dragon leaving the sea with not the slightest thing obstructing it” (如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). He warns against mistaking the wording for reckless indulgence. A community rule likewise attacks “taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease” (將狂妄作逍遙). A direct question about “a person roaming at ease outside things” receives the answer “red and festering all over, unable to be supported” (遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Roaming through mountains and valleys (逍遙山谷) is verb plus object and remains here, not under the place name.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs also name a Chan master. Independent lineage notices identify Master Xiaoyao as a successor of Jiashan and locate him at Gao'an. His preserved record has him seated on the Chan seat; in the encounter with Luxi he strikes Luxi across the mouth with the fly-whisk and then addresses the assembly. This personal name is a different referent from roaming at ease.
Senses.Note: Master Xiaoyao is absent from the current canonical master roster, so the sense and occurrences remain unlinked rather than assigning an invented canonical name. He is not Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao: the lineage notice makes Xiaoyao Jiashan's successor, while the mountain headings explicitly name Huaizhong.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The heading says, ‘Master Xiaoyao.’ The record continues, ‘One day the master was sitting on the Chan seat.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 逍遙和尚○逍遙嗣夾山，在高安。未睹行錄，不決始終。

Senses.Explanation: In Chan master headings the graphs also form the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Independent compilations name “Chan Master Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao in Jiangxi” (江西逍遙山懷忠禪師). The mountain is the monastery location attached to Huaizhong, not Master Xiaoyao and not the act of roaming.
Senses.Note: Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao is absent from the current canonical master roster, so the person is translated in prose but not entered as an unverified RelatedMasters value. Roaming through mountains and valleys (逍遙山谷) is ordinary verb-plus-object syntax and is excluded from this place sense.
